blurb: Wiry see-through stems hold short, dense drumstick heads of deep maroon to blackish-purple from midsummer into fall — the colour comes from sepals and stamens, since the flowers have no petals at all — over a low clump of blue-green pinnate leaflets. A New Perennial and prairie-style staple for movement and late structure, whose spent heads dry to rusty seedheads that stand well into winter. But make no mistake: this is a wet-meadow plant, and Boulder is not a wet meadow.
size: ~2–4 ft tall × 1.5–3 ft wide (flower stems to 5 ft on rich, constantly moist ground; dwarf forms like 'Tanna' stay ~1.5–2 ft)
sun: Full sun to part shade — full sun here only where the soil stays genuinely moist; afternoon shade otherwise
water: High — wants consistently moist soil; a wet-meadow species that scorches, stalls and browns out in dry Front Range beds. Not a xeric plant, and a real water cost here.
spread: Clump-forming but rhizomatous — creeps steadily outward in moist ground, and the species self-seeds freely unless spent heads are cut
seasons: Blue-green pinnate basal foliage emerging in spring; maroon-to-burgundy drumstick heads on airy stems from midsummer into fall; the spent heads dry to rusty seedheads that hold their shape through winter if left standing
wildlife: An RHS 'Plants for Pollinators' selection — bees and other insects work the heads; in Europe it is the sole larval host of the endangered large blue butterflies (Phengaris teleius and P. nausithous), a relationship that does not exist in Colorado
toxic: No significant toxicity reported to people or pets; the root is a high-tannin traditional medicine (Di Yu), not a food
origin: Cool-temperate Eurasia — Europe through northern Asia; circumboreal, with scattered native North American populations in Alaska, the Pacific Northwest and the far Northeast, but none in Colorado
habitat: Damp meadows, fens and grassy streamsides on moist to wet soils (a facultative-wetland species)

care.hardiness: Cold is the easy part here: it is rated USDA 4–8 and carries the RHS's top H7 hardiness rating (hardy below −20 °C), so Boulder's zone 5b–6a winters are no threat at all.[1][2] The limit at our end is heat and dryness, not cold — zone 8 is the warm edge of its range, and our intense high-altitude sun and low humidity push it hard in July and August.[1][2]
care.planting: Set container-grown plants out any time in the growing season, though spring after the mid-May last frost or early fall gives the roots the coolest, wettest weeks to establish; bare-root divisions are best planted in spring.[5] Site it deliberately where water collects or where you already irrigate — a low spot, a downspout run, a rain-garden edge, or the wet end of a drip line — because it grows in damp meadows and streamside grassland and is classed a facultative-wetland plant.[2][3][4] It is a poor long-term container subject: pots on the Front Range dry out far faster than this plant tolerates, so if you must pot it use a big container with a moisture-retentive mix and expect to water daily in summer.[2][5]
care.sun: Grows in full sun or partial shade.[2] In Boulder, full sun is only honest advice where the soil stays genuinely moist — in an ordinary dry bed the combination of high-altitude sun and dry air scorches the leaf margins, so give it afternoon shade unless you are watering it properly.[2][8] Too much shade, though, and the tall stems stretch and flop.[2]
care.soil: Tolerates chalk, clay, loam and sand across acid, neutral and alkaline pH, so Boulder's alkaline clay is not a problem — the clay's water-holding capacity is actually an asset for this plant.[2][8] What it wants is moderately fertile, moisture-retentive ground; work compost or other organic matter about 12 inches deep before planting to improve both structure and water retention.[2][5] Avoid the rich-plus-shady combination: fertile soil out of full sun produces lax growth that flops.[1][2]
care.water: This is the make-or-break field. Great burnet grows wild in wet grassy places by streams and on fen meadows, and is rated FACW — it usually occurs in wetlands.[3][4][8] Boulder's semi-arid, fast-draining ground gives it nothing like that, so plan on a deep soak once or twice a week through summer (more in a heat wave), delivered by drip and held in by 2–3 inches of mulch, which reduces water loss and keeps plants from drying out as fast.[5][8] Let it go dry and it does not simply sulk — leaf margins brown, flowering stalls, and the clump can go dormant early. Be plain with yourself about this: it is a real water cost in a dry climate, and it does not belong in a xeriscape or an unirrigated bed.[3][4][8]
care.spacing: Space plants about 18–24 in apart, allowing for a mature spread of roughly 1.5–3 ft, and give them room — overcrowded perennials bloom poorly.[1][5] The rhizomes will knit the gaps closed on their own in moist ground, so err toward the wider spacing rather than the tighter one.[2]
care.propagation: Divide established clumps in spring or autumn — the simplest and quickest route, and the only way to keep named forms like 'Tanna' or 'Red Thunder' true.[2] Seed also works, sown in pots in a cold frame in spring or autumn.[2] The straight species self-seeds freely, so the laziest method of all is to lift the volunteer seedlings that appear around a happy plant; deadheading is what stops that from getting out of hand.[1] Plan on lifting and dividing every three to five growing seasons anyway, doing it when the plant is not blooming.[5]
care.sow: Sow into pots in a cold frame in spring or autumn; an autumn sowing set outdoors lets our winter supply the cold, moist period naturally, and pots must never be allowed to dry out.[2] Given how freely the species self-sows, transplanting volunteer seedlings in spring is usually faster than raising a flat from seed.[1]
care.bloom: Short, dense oblong heads — to about 1.5 in — of dark red to blackish-purple open through summer and into early autumn, roughly June through September here, peaking midsummer.[1][2][4] The flowers have no petals: what you see is coloured sepals with the stamens showing through.[3][4] Removing spent blooms is worth doing, both because it tidies the plant and because it prevents excessive self-seeding.[1]
care.feeding: Needs very little. Moderately fertile soil is the target, and a spring topdressing of compost is plenty.[2] Skip the fertilizer — feeding a plant that is already inclined to lean produces soft, tall growth that flops and needs staking.[1][2]
care.maintenance: Expect to support it: the RHS notes it usually requires support, and MBG warns that taller specimens may need staking, so slip a grow-through hoop or a ring of pea-stakes over the clump in late spring before the stems get away from you — far easier than tying up a collapsed plant in August.[1][2] Growing it in full sun on unfertilized soil produces the sturdiest stems.[1][2] Leave the rusty seedheads standing over winter for structure and for wildlife — less fall cutback and cleanup is now the recommended practice, except where pest or disease is present — then cut everything to the ground in late winter before new growth pushes.[5] Watch the rhizomes: they can spread readily and become problematic, so site it with care and edge or divide it back every few years.[2][5]
care.troubles: Genuinely pest- and disease-free in most gardens, with no significant insect or disease problems reported.[1][2] Nearly every failure here traces to one of two things: drought stress (scorched leaf margins, aborted flowering, early dormancy) in our dry, fast-draining ground, or flopping stems from rich soil, too much shade, or too much fertilizer.[1][2][8] Neither is a disease — both are siting mistakes.
care.companions: MBG lists it for borders, herb gardens and naturalizing, and its see-through, late-season habit is what makes it a prairie-style and New Perennial staple.[1] Design its bed around its water demand rather than fighting it: put it with other things that want steady moisture — swamp milkweed, Rocky Mountain iris, switchgrass, Japanese anemone — so one irrigation zone serves them all, and keep it well away from xeric companions that will rot on that schedule.[2][3][5] Plan the planting with mature sizes in mind and leave adequate room for growth.[5]

edible.card: Young spring leaves & buds, raw or cooked (salad, soup, tea)
edible.summary: Young leaves and flower buds have documented food use — mild, faintly cucumber-flavoured in salads, soups or as a tea — but this plant is far better known as the high-tannin Chinese medicinal Di Yu, so treat it as a garden nibble rather than a crop.[1][6][8]
edible.parts: The young leaves are the edible part: MBG describes younger leaves as excellent in salads and soups, and the pharmacological literature records that fresh leaves from young plants are used as a seasoning for salads and meat dishes.[1][6] Young leaves and flower buds gathered in spring before flowering are eaten raw or cooked, with a cucumber flavour, and fresh or dried leaves are used as a tea substitute.[8] The root is NOT a food — it is the medicinal part (Sanguisorbae Radix, Di Yu), harvested in spring or autumn and used in traditional Chinese medicine, not in the kitchen.[6][9]
edible.preparation: Pick only the young, tender spring leaves and unopened buds before the plant flowers; older leaves turn tough and astringent as tannin builds.[8] Wash and use them raw in small quantity in a mixed salad, add them to soups as a potherb, or steep fresh or dried leaves as a tea.[1][8] Treat it as a seasoning green in modest amounts, not as a bulk salad base.[6][8]
edible.caution: The whole plant is astringent and tannin-rich — that astringency is precisely what its medicine is built on, and it is the reason older leaves are unpleasant and large quantities are a bad idea.[6][8] Do not read the medicinal record as a food recommendation: the root is a traditional Chinese medicine used to stop bleeding and treat wounds, burns and dysentery, and medicinal, dose-controlled use of a herbal preparation is a different thing entirely from eating a plant.[6][8][9] Safety data are thin: a comprehensive review of the genus found no harmful components such as alkaloids reported in S. officinalis, but the same review states plainly that reports on harmful ingredients, organ toxicity and the safety of Sanguisorba are scarce — absence of evidence, not evidence of safety.[6] PFAF advises it is best avoided during pregnancy given the lack of toxicity information, and notes the herb may interact with fluoroquinolone antibiotics.[8] Anyone pregnant, nursing, or taking medication should leave it alone. Finally, know which burnet you have — great burnet is the tall, dark-red-headed border plant, not the low culinary salad burnet (S. minor) that is the genus's actual kitchen herb — and never eat nursery or ornamental stock that may have been treated with pesticides.[6][8]
